CHAPTER 4.1 · LEARNING AREA 4

CHAPTER 4.1 · LEARNING AREA 4 · APRIL · MAY

Probability and counting

What does “probable” actually mean? You meet three answers: the statistical one through long series of trials, the one by Laplace through equally likely outcomes and the one by Kolmogorov through three axioms from which all the rules of calculation can be proved. Then you break multi-stage random experiments down with urn, tree and two-way table and count large sets of outcomes cleverly, with the factorial and the binomial coefficient.

13 LESSONS3 UNITS3 PRACTICE PAGESCOUNTING
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • to distinguish the statistical, Laplace’s and the axiomatic notion of probability and to prove rules of calculation from the axioms
  • to simulate random experiments and to judge how accurate a simulation is
  • to represent multi-stage random experiments with the urn model, the tree diagram and the two-way table and to calculate with the path rules
  • to count outcomes with the product rule, the factorial and the binomial coefficient

Two favourable out of six equally likely outcomes: $\tfrac26 = \tfrac13$ (Year 10).

A dice is rolled twice. What is the complementary event of “at least one 6”?

“At least one” is false exactly when no 6 is rolled at all.

Work out $\tfrac35 \cdot \tfrac24$ as a decimal.

$\tfrac{6}{20} = 0.3$

A coin is tossed twice. What is the probability of heads twice?

$\tfrac12 \cdot \tfrac12 = \tfrac14$

UNIT 14 LESSONS

1Approaches to the notion of probability

With a dice everyone says at once: the probability of a 6 is $\tfrac16$, because no face is favoured. A drawing pin does not have this symmetry. Here only trying helps: if you throw it very often, the proportion of landings on its back settles down at a fixed value. And what is a probability, really? Mathematics has an astonishingly short answer: three rules.

KEY POINT · THREE APPROACHES

Statistical: if an event $E$ occurs $H_n(E)$ times in $n$ trials, then $h_n(E) = \tfrac{H_n(E)}{n}$ is its relative frequency. For large $n$ it settles down (empirical law of large numbers). It is an estimate of $P(E)$.

Laplace: if a random experiment has finitely many equally likely outcomes, then $P(E) = \dfrac{|E|}{|\Omega|} = \dfrac{\text{number of favourable outcomes}}{\text{number of possible outcomes}}$.

Kolmogorov (axiomatic): a probability assigns to every event $E \subseteq \Omega$ a number $P(E)$ with
(K1) $P(E) \ge 0$, (K2) $P(\Omega) = 1$, (K3) $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B)$ if $A \cap B = \emptyset$ (mutually exclusive events).

Consequences: $P(\overline{E}) = 1 - P(E)$, $P(\emptyset) = 0$ and the addition rule $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)$.

Proof for the complementary event: $E$ and $\overline{E}$ are mutually exclusive, and $E \cup \overline{E} = \Omega$. With (K3) and (K2): $P(E) + P(\overline{E}) = 1$.

Laplace only with symmetry: the totals $2, 3, \ldots, 12$ of two dice are not equally likely. Equally likely are the 36 pairs $(1, 1), \ldots, (6, 6)$.

Source: Andrei N. Kolmogorov: “Grundbegriffe der Wahrscheinlichkeitsrechnung” (Foundations of the Theory of Probability), Springer, Berlin 1933. In about 60 pages he turned probability into a theory built on axioms, like geometry.

INTERACTIVE · THE LAW OF LARGE NUMBERS

Choose a random experiment and let it run 10, 100 or 1000 times. The relative frequency fluctuates strongly at first and then approaches the probability.

EXAMPLE 1 · TWO DICE

Two dice are rolled. Calculate the probabilities of the total 7 and of a total of at least 10.

Laplace model with the 36 equally likely pairs. Total 7: $(1, 6), (2, 5), \ldots, (6, 1)$, so 6 pairs and $P = \tfrac{6}{36} = \tfrac16$.

Total at least 10: total 10 has 3 pairs, 11 has 2 and 12 has 1. $P = \tfrac{6}{36} = \tfrac16$.

EXAMPLE 2 · THE ADDITION RULE FROM THE AXIOMS

Prove $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)$ and use it to calculate, for one card from a skat deck (32 cards), the probability of “hearts or jack”.

$A \cup B$ splits into the mutually exclusive parts $A$ and $B \setminus A$; likewise $B$ into $A \cap B$ and $B \setminus A$. By (K3), $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B \setminus A)$ and $P(B) = P(A \cap B) + P(B \setminus A)$. Substituting $P(B \setminus A) = P(B) - P(A \cap B)$ gives the rule.

8 hearts, 4 jacks, 1 jack of hearts: $P = \tfrac{8}{32} + \tfrac{4}{32} - \tfrac{1}{32} = \tfrac{11}{32} \approx 0.344$.

EXERCISES

In 400 throws a drawing pin landed on its back 248 times. Estimate the probability of this and explain why no Laplace model fits here.

$h_{400} = \tfrac{248}{400} = 0.62$ is the estimate. Landing on the back and on the side are not symmetrical, so they are not equally likely.

Two dice: calculate the probability of a double and of at least one 6.

Double: 6 of 36 pairs, $P = \tfrac16$. At least one 6: via the complementary event, $1 - \tfrac{25}{36} = \tfrac{11}{36} \approx 0.306$.

Prove with the axioms: $A \subseteq B$ implies $P(A) \le P(B)$.

$B = A \cup (B \setminus A)$ with mutually exclusive parts. By (K3), $P(B) = P(A) + P(B \setminus A)$, and by (K1), $P(B \setminus A) \ge 0$. So $P(B) \ge P(A)$.

We have $P(A) = 0.5$, $P(B) = 0.4$ and $P(A \cup B) = 0.7$. Calculate $P(A \cap B)$ and the probability that only $A$ occurs.

Addition rule: $P(A \cap B) = 0.5 + 0.4 - 0.7 = 0.2$. Only $A$: $P(A \setminus B) = 0.5 - 0.2 = 0.3$.

A spreadsheet gives uniformly distributed random numbers $z$ from $[0, 1)$. How do you simulate a dice with them? Roughly how many simulations do you need so that the relative frequency of a probability around $0.5$ is usually correct to $\pm 0.01$?

Score $\lfloor 6z \rfloor + 1$, for example with =INT(6*RAND())+1. The relative frequency fluctuates around $P$ with the standard deviation $\sqrt{\tfrac{P(1 - P)}{n}} \le \tfrac{0.5}{\sqrt n}$. For about $95\%$ certainty, twice the fluctuation should be at most $0.01$: $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt n} \le 0.01$, so $n \ge 10{,}000$.

TEST YOURSELF!

Two dice: what is the probability of the total 9?

$(3, 6), (4, 5), (5, 4), (6, 3)$: $\tfrac{4}{36} = \tfrac19$

$A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive, $P(A) = 0.3$ and $P(B) = 0.5$. What is $P(A \cup B)$?

(K3): $0.3 + 0.5 = 0.8$

In 2000 rolls a dice showed the 6 a total of 380 times. What is the relative frequency?

$\tfrac{380}{2000} = 0.19$, clearly above $\tfrac16 \approx 0.167$: the dice is suspicious.

UNIT 25 LESSONS

2Multi-stage random experiments

Two balls are drawn from the urn with three red and two blue balls. If the first is not put back, the urn changes for the second draw. A tree diagram records this: it branches at every stage, and on the branches you write the probabilities given what happened before.

KEY POINT · PATH RULES AND TWO-WAY TABLE

1st path rule (product rule): the probability of a path is the product of the probabilities along the path.

2nd path rule (sum rule): the probability of an event is the sum of the probabilities of all the paths that belong to it.

Urn model: when drawing with replacement the probabilities stay the same at every stage, when drawing without replacement they change from stage to stage.

Two-way table: for two characteristics $A$ and $B$ the four cells hold $P(A \cap B)$, $P(A \cap \overline{B})$, $P(\overline{A} \cap B)$, $P(\overline{A} \cap \overline{B})$, the margins hold the sums $P(A)$, $P(\overline{A})$, $P(B)$, $P(\overline{B})$ and the bottom right holds $1$.

Check: the probabilities of all the path ends add up to $1$, and so do the branches leaving each node.

The complementary event saves paths: at least one 6 in four rolls: $1 - \left(\tfrac56\right)^4 \approx 0.518$. Without the complementary event it would be 15 paths.

Table or tree? Both contain the same four intersection probabilities. The table shows all the sums at a glance, the tree the order of the stages.

INTERACTIVE · TREE DIAGRAM WORKSHOP

Set up the urn, choose with or without replacement and click on the path ends or an event. The path rules calculate along.

EXAMPLE 3 · WITH OR WITHOUT REPLACEMENT

Two balls are drawn from the urn with three red and two blue balls. Calculate $P(\text{two different colours})$ without and with replacement.

Without replacement, paths $rb$ and $br$: $\tfrac35 \cdot \tfrac24 + \tfrac25 \cdot \tfrac34 = \tfrac{6}{20} + \tfrac{6}{20} = \tfrac35 = 0.6$.

With replacement: $2 \cdot \tfrac35 \cdot \tfrac25 = \tfrac{12}{25} = 0.48$. Without replacement “different” is more likely. The first ball is then missing from the urn, and the other colour becomes relatively more frequent.

EXAMPLE 4 · TWO-WAY TABLE

Of 200 students, 80 live outside the town ($A$); of these, 60 go by bus ($B$). Of the others, 30 go by bus. Set up the two-way table and find $P(B)$ and $P(\overline{A} \cap \overline{B})$ for a student chosen at random.

$B$$\overline{B}$$\Sigma$
$A$602080
$\overline{A}$3090120
$\Sigma$90110200

$P(B) = \tfrac{90}{200} = 0.45$ and $P(\overline{A} \cap \overline{B}) = \tfrac{90}{200} = 0.45$.

EXERCISES

A coin is tossed and a dice is rolled. What is the probability of heads and an even score?

Path heads, even: $\tfrac12 \cdot \tfrac12 = \tfrac14$.

An urn contains 4 red and 6 white balls. Two are drawn without replacement. Calculate $P(\text{two red})$ and $P(\text{at least one white})$.

$\tfrac{4}{10} \cdot \tfrac39 = \tfrac{12}{90} = \tfrac{2}{15} \approx 0.133$. At least one white is the complementary event: $1 - \tfrac{2}{15} = \tfrac{13}{15} \approx 0.867$.

From an urn with 2 red and 3 blue balls, three balls are drawn with replacement. What is the probability of exactly two red balls?

Three paths $rrb$, $rbr$, $brr$, each with $\left(\tfrac25\right)^2 \cdot \tfrac35 = \tfrac{12}{125}$. Together $\tfrac{36}{125} = 0.288$.

Complete the two-way table with $P(A) = 0.4$, $P(B) = 0.3$ and $P(A \cap B) = 0.1$.

$P(A \cap \overline{B}) = 0.3$, $P(\overline{A} \cap B) = 0.2$, $P(\overline{A} \cap \overline{B}) = 0.6 - 0.2 = 0.4$; margins $P(\overline{A}) = 0.6$, $P(\overline{B}) = 0.7$.

From the urn with three red and two blue balls you draw without replacement until the first blue ball appears. How likely is it that you draw exactly three times? With what probability do you need at most two draws?

Exactly three draws means $rrb$: $\tfrac35 \cdot \tfrac24 \cdot \tfrac23 = \tfrac{12}{60} = \tfrac15$. At most two: $b$ or $rb$, so $\tfrac25 + \tfrac35 \cdot \tfrac24 = \tfrac25 + \tfrac{3}{10} = \tfrac{7}{10}$.

TEST YOURSELF!

Two balls are drawn without replacement from 5 red and 5 blue balls. What is $P(\text{two of the same colour})$?

$2 \cdot \tfrac{5}{10} \cdot \tfrac49 = \tfrac{40}{90} = \tfrac49 \approx 0.444$

A dice is rolled three times. What is the probability that no 6 appears (three decimal places)?

$\left(\tfrac56\right)^3 = \tfrac{125}{216} \approx 0.579$

$P(A) = 0.6$, $P(B) = 0.5$, $P(A \cap B) = 0.45$. What is $P(\overline{A} \cap \overline{B})$?

$P(A \cup B) = 0.65$, so $P(\overline{A} \cap \overline{B}) = 1 - 0.65 = 0.35$.

UNIT 34 LESSONS

3Counting methods

A bike lock has three rings with ten digits each: $10 \cdot 10 \cdot 10 = 1000$ settings. For the lottery “6 from 49” nobody would draw a tree with 49 branches at the first node any more. But for Laplace probabilities you only have to count, and that works with a few rules.

KEY POINT · COUNTING IN THE URN MODEL

Product rule: if a process has $k$ stages with $n_1, n_2, \ldots, n_k$ possibilities, there are $n_1 \cdot n_2 \cdot \ldots \cdot n_k$ outcomes.

From an urn with $n$ distinguishable balls, $k$ balls are drawn:

  • with replacement, order matters: $n^k$
  • without replacement, order matters: $n \cdot (n - 1) \cdot \ldots \cdot (n - k + 1) = \dfrac{n!}{(n - k)!}$
  • without replacement, order does not matter: $\dbinom{n}{k} = \dfrac{n!}{k! \cdot (n - k)!}$ (binomial coefficient, read “$n$ choose $k$”)

Factorial: $n! = 1 \cdot 2 \cdot \ldots \cdot n$ is the number of arrangements of $n$ things; $0! = 1$.

Why divide by $k!$? Every selection of $k$ balls appears exactly $k!$ times among the ordered draws, in every possible order.

Symmetry: $\binom{n}{k} = \binom{n}{n - k}$, because whoever chooses $k$ balls fixes the $n - k$ remaining ones at the same time.

Calculator: the binomial coefficient is usually called nCr, the factorial n!. Even $70!$ is greater than $10^{100}$.

INTERACTIVE · THE URN

Choose the number of balls and draws, with or without order and replacement. The widget shows the formula, the number and, for small numbers, all the outcomes.

EXAMPLE 5 · LOTTERY 6 FROM 49

How many tickets are there? How likely are six correct numbers, and how likely exactly three?

Without replacement, order does not matter: $\binom{49}{6} = 13{,}983{,}816$ equally likely tickets, so $P(6\ \text{correct}) = \tfrac{1}{13{,}983{,}816} \approx 7.2 \cdot 10^{-8}$.

Exactly three correct: 3 of the 6 winning numbers and 3 of the 43 others, $\binom63 \cdot \binom{43}{3} = 20 \cdot 12{,}341 = 246{,}820$ tickets. $P = \tfrac{246{,}820}{13{,}983{,}816} \approx 0.0177$, so about every 57th ticket.

EXAMPLE 6 · THE BIRTHDAY PROBLEM

There are 23 people in a class. What is the probability that at least two of them share a birthday? Work with 365 equally likely days.

Complementary event “all different”: ordered without replacement, $365 \cdot 364 \cdot \ldots \cdot 343$ favourable out of $365^{23}$ possible outcomes.

$P(\text{all different}) = \dfrac{365!}{342! \cdot 365^{23}} \approx 0.4927$, so $P(\text{at least two the same}) \approx 0.5073$. As few as 23 people are enough for more than $50\%$, because there are $\binom{23}{2} = 253$ pairs.

INTERACTIVE · THE BIRTHDAY PROBLEM

Set the number of people. The curve shows the probability of at least one shared birthday, and the simulation checks it on a thousand classes.

EXERCISES

How many four-digit PINs are there? How many of them have four different digits?

$10^4 = 10{,}000$; with different digits $10 \cdot 9 \cdot 8 \cdot 7 = 5040$.

In how many ways can six people stand in a row?

$6! = 720$

A team of three is chosen from 20 people. How many teams are there? How many possibilities are there if the three take on the roles of chair, deputy and treasurer?

Without order $\binom{20}{3} = 1140$; with roles the order matters: $20 \cdot 19 \cdot 18 = 6840 = 3! \cdot 1140$.

In skat each player gets 10 of the 32 cards. What is the probability of getting all four jacks?

$\dfrac{\binom44 \cdot \binom{28}{6}}{\binom{32}{10}} = \dfrac{376{,}740}{64{,}512{,}240} \approx 0.0058$

Prove by counting: $\binom{n}{k} = \binom{n - 1}{k - 1} + \binom{n - 1}{k}$ for $1 \le k \le n - 1$. What does this have to do with Pascal’s triangle?

Mark one of the $n$ balls. The selections of $k$ balls either contain it (then $k - 1$ are still missing from the other $n - 1$: $\binom{n - 1}{k - 1}$) or not (all $k$ from the others: $\binom{n - 1}{k}$). In Pascal’s triangle this is the rule: every number is the sum of the two above it.

TEST YOURSELF!

What is $\binom73$?

$\tfrac{7 \cdot 6 \cdot 5}{3!} = 35$

In how many ways can you hang 3 of 8 pictures side by side on a wall?

With order, without repetition: $8 \cdot 7 \cdot 6 = 336$

From 5 red and 3 blue balls, 3 are drawn without replacement. What is $P(\text{exactly two red})$?

$\dfrac{\binom52 \cdot \binom31}{\binom83} = \dfrac{30}{56} = \dfrac{15}{28} \approx 0.536$

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

A test has 5 questions with 4 answers each, exactly one of which is right. How likely is it to get everything right by pure guessing? How likely is at least one right answer?

$\left(\tfrac14\right)^5 = \tfrac{1}{1024} \approx 0.001$. At least one right: $1 - \left(\tfrac34\right)^5 = 1 - \tfrac{243}{1024} = \tfrac{781}{1024} \approx 0.763$.

Connecting with biology: two parents are heterozygous $Aa$ for a recessively inherited trait. Each child receives the allele $a$ from each parent with probability $\tfrac12$. How likely is a child with $aa$? How likely is it that at least one of three children has $aa$?

$P(aa) = \tfrac12 \cdot \tfrac12 = \tfrac14$. For three children via the complementary event: $1 - \left(\tfrac34\right)^3 = \tfrac{37}{64} \approx 0.578$.

How many different outcomes does rolling three distinguishable dice have? What is the probability that all three scores are different?

$6^3 = 216$ outcomes; different: $6 \cdot 5 \cdot 4 = 120$, so $\tfrac{120}{216} = \tfrac59 \approx 0.556$.

A supplier claims that at most 2 of the 20 devices in a box are faulty. You test 4 devices chosen at random and find none faulty. How likely is this result if exactly 2 really are faulty? What does that say about the claim?

Without replacement: $\dfrac{\binom{18}{4}}{\binom{20}{4}} = \dfrac{3060}{4845} \approx 0.632$. So the result fits the claim well, but it does not prove it. You will learn how to make such decisions properly in the inferential statistics of Year 12.

EXCURSIONHISTORY

The interrupted game

In the summer of 1654 two Frenchmen wrote each other letters about a question gamblers had argued about for centuries: two players each stake 32 pistoles (gold coins). Whoever first wins three rounds gets all 64. At a score of $2:1$ the game has to be stopped. How is the stake divided fairly?

Older proposals, for example by Luca Pacioli in 1494, divided according to the rounds already won, that is $2:1$. Blaise Pascal and Pierre de Fermat looked forward instead: if the leader wins the next round, he has all 64; if he loses, it is $2:2$ and each has the same chance, so 32. With $\tfrac12$ each, he is entitled to $\tfrac12 \cdot 64 + \tfrac12 \cdot 32 = 48$ pistoles, the other to 16.

Fermat calculated differently and counted: after at most two more rounds everything is decided. The four equally likely continuations are $AA$, $AB$, $BA$, $BB$; only with $BB$ does the player behind win. So the leader gets $\tfrac34$ of the stake. Both ways lead to $48:16$. With this exchange of letters probability theory begins as mathematics.

Source: letter from Blaise Pascal to Pierre de Fermat of 29 July 1654, with exactly this example (32 pistoles, three winning rounds).

Work it out: score $2:0$ with three winning rounds. Show with Fermat’s counting (up to three more rounds) that the leader is entitled to $\tfrac78$.

LOOKING BACKTHE ESSENTIALS AT A GLANCE

THREE APPROACHES

Relative frequency as an estimate; Laplace $\tfrac{|E|}{|\Omega|}$ for equally likely outcomes; axioms (K1) to (K3) after Kolmogorov.

Drawing pin: $h_{400} = 0.62$; total 7: $\tfrac{6}{36}$

RULES OF CALCULATION

$P(\overline{E}) = 1 - P(E)$; addition rule $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)$.

Hearts or jack: $\tfrac{8 + 4 - 1}{32} = \tfrac{11}{32}$

PATH RULES

Multiply along a path, add the paths of an event; without replacement the branches change.

Two different colours: $\tfrac35 \cdot \tfrac24 + \tfrac25 \cdot \tfrac34 = \tfrac35$

TWO-WAY TABLE

Four intersection probabilities, margin sums, $1$ at the bottom right.

$P(\overline{A} \cap \overline{B}) = 1 - P(A \cup B)$

COUNTING

$n^k$; $\tfrac{n!}{(n - k)!}$; $\binom{n}{k} = \tfrac{n!}{k!\,(n - k)!}$; $n!$ arrangements.

Lottery: $\binom{49}{6} = 13{,}983{,}816$
